articles.title: NASA just powered up Roman’s massive 300-megapixel camera
articles.description: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has successfully activated its 300-megapixel infrared camera, which will capture enormous stretches of the cosmos with Hubble-like sharpness. Its planet-hunting coronagraph is also working as expected, putting Roman another major step closer to beginning science operations in 2027.
articles.summary: NASA's Roman Space Telescope has successfully activated its groundbreaking 300-megapixel infrared camera, a major milestone for this flagship mission.

articles.title: NASA Discovery Reveals Complex Water Systems on Early Mars
articles.description: When NASA’s Perseverance rover reached the inner edge of Mars’ Jezero Crater in September 2023, mission scientists were surprised by what they found. Called the “Margin Unit,” the geologic area stretches along the shoreline of an ancient Martian lake, so they expected sedimentary rocks, which would have formed as layers of sand piled on top […]
articles.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover reveals evidence of complex water systems that existed on early Mars, deepening our understanding of the planet's past habitability.

articles.title: Webb reveals stunning panorama of star formation
articles.description: This starry view of the nearby star-forming region IC 348 is one of the largest images from the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope released to the public so far. Using Webb, astronomers searched IC 348 for brown dwarfs, which are less massive than the smallest stars. The researchers discovered brown dwarfs just twice the mass of Jupiter, bringing the study of these curious objects into a new mass range.
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope unveils a breathtaking panoramic view of star formation in the nearby IC 348 region, capturing one of the largest images from the observatory.

articles.title: BepiColombo begins Mercury arrival with MTM separation success
articles.description: On 3 September 2026 at 15:49 CEST, the European Space Agency's BepiColombo Mission Control Team at the European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) received the signal they had been waiting for – BepiColombo’s Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) successfully separated from the spacecraft stack. This landmark achievement for the ESA and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission marks the first step of BepiColombo's long-awaited arrival at Mercury.
articles.summary: ESA's BepiColombo successfully completes Mercury Transfer Module separation, marking a major milestone as the spacecraft begins its Mercury arrival sequence.

articles.title: Hubble tracks new decagon encircling Saturn’s south pole
articles.description: Recent observations with the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope have revealed a giant, evolving 10-sided atmospheric wave encircling Saturn’s south pole. This discovery marks the first time a large regular-sided jet pattern has been observed in the planet’s southern hemisphere. The feature appears remarkably similar to Saturn’s famous hexagon at its northern pole, but is also distinctly different, suggesting scientists may be witnessing a new atmospheric phenomenon develop on the iconic gas giant.
articles.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope has discovered a remarkable 10-sided atmospheric wave circling Saturn's south pole, revealing the dynamic complexity of the gas giant's atmosphere.

articles.title: Solar Orbiter Catches the Sun’s Missing High-Speed Vibrations
articles.description: The Sun’s magnetic fields are a twisty, curvy, ever changing mess. In particular, our star’s polar regions host regions called polar coronal holes that host invisible magnetic highways that stretch out into interplanetary space. But there’s a lot we don’t know about how those highways actually work, and in particular how they give the particles that form the fast solar wind an extra “kick” that sends them zooming at hundreds of kilometers per second. A new paper from a team led by Dr. Yuhang Gao and Prof. Hui Tian at Peking University, and published recently in the journal National Science Review, thinks they might have found an answer by using high-speed shots from Solar Orbiter to detect never-before seen rapid, high-frequency magnetic waves in those areas.
articles.summary: The Solar Orbiter has detected the Sun's previously elusive high-speed vibrations in its polar regions, deepening our understanding of solar magnetic field behavior.

articles.title: MIT Research Could Lead to Refueling Depots on Mars
articles.description: MIT PhD candidate Lanie McKinney is developing technology to convert the chemicals in the Martian atmosphere into propellant to bring astronauts home.
articles.summary: MIT researchers are developing technology to extract and convert Martian atmospheric chemicals into fuel, potentially enabling sustainable refueling depots for future Mars missions.

articles.title: Researchers Measure the Environment Where the First Supermassive Black Holes Formed
articles.description: Scientists theorize that the rapid emergence of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in the early Universe can be explained by the direct-collapse black hole (DCBH) scenario. In a recent study, astronomers investigated the potential host environments of DCBHs and found that this scenario is a plausible explanation for how the "seeds" of SMBH formed.
articles.summary: Scientists have measured the environment where the first supermassive black holes formed in the early universe, shedding light on one of cosmology's greatest mysteries.

articles.title: Student-led missions deploy free-flying light sails from CubeSats in low Earth orbit
articles.description: Students in Cornell's Space Systems Design Studio (SSDS) have released mission results for two unique light-sail experiments. These sails are slightly larger than a pizza box and harness momentum from photons to accelerate to high velocities. With ChipSats onboard—gram-scale spacecraft that fit in the palm of your hand—the sails can become free-flyers. They origami-fold into CubeSats for launch and completely separate when deployed, allowing them to be far smaller and lighter than traditional solar sails. The ChipSats provide all ground communications and steering capabilities for a fraction of the mass and cost.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Cornell University students have successfully deployed innovative free-flying light sails from CubeSats in orbit, advancing experimental propulsion technology for future spacecraft.

articles.title: Early Mars rocks reveal at least three separate water episodes
articles.description: When NASA's Perseverance rover reached the inner edge of Mars' Jezero Crater in September 2023, mission scientists were surprised by what they found. The geologic area, called the "Margin Unit," stretches along the shoreline of an ancient Martian lake, so they expected sedimentary rocks, which would have formed as layers of sand piled on top of each other over millennia. Composed of clay and silt, sedimentary rocks on Earth are good at preserving past microbial life. The scientists were especially intrigued by strong signals of carbonate minerals detected by Mars orbiters. On Earth, carbonates frequently form in shallow ocean and lake environments capable of supporting life.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover has discovered evidence of at least three distinct water episodes in Mars' Jezero Crater, revealing a complex hydrological history on early Mars.

articles.title: Superdense neutron star caught feeding on a blue hypergiant's stellar wind
articles.description: Using data from the Japan–led XRISM (X-ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission) observatory, astronomers have directly observed a giant star's outflow, called a stellar wind, being captured by its compact companion and providing the power source for strong X-ray flares. The research is part of NASA's exploration of the extreme universe to better understand how the cosmos works.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: The XRISM observatory has captured detailed observations of a neutron star actively feeding on stellar wind from a blue hypergiant companion, revealing extreme cosmic processes.

articles.title: Black holes of every size follow the same surprising rule
articles.description: Scientists have found evidence that black holes of vastly different sizes may launch powerful jets according to the same universal rule. Supermassive black holes can produce jets soon after tearing apart a star, then fire up again hundreds or thousands of days later when their feeding rate drops to about 2% of the Eddington limit. That same threshold is known to trigger jets from much smaller black holes in the Milky Way.
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that black holes of vastly different sizes launch powerful jets according to the same underlying physical rule, revealing a fundamental principle of the universe.

articles.title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope could last more than twice as long as planned
articles.description: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope may now have enough fuel for at least 22 years of science, more than double its original 10 year design life. An extremely precise course correction, extra fuel at launch, and additional expected savings could keep the powerful observatory studying the universe for decades.
articles.summary: NASA's Roman Space Telescope may now operate for at least 22 years, more than double its original planned mission duration, expanding its scientific potential.

articles.title: Astronomers Confirm Youngest Known Planet, Less Than 1 Million Years Old
articles.description: Astronomers have confirmed the youngest known planet yet, a Jupiter-size world less than 1 million years old that orbits a star about 450 light-years from Earth, according to a study published Sept. 16 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. The planet, designa…
articles.summary: Astronomers have confirmed the youngest known planet ever discovered, a Jupiter-sized world less than 1 million years old still forming around its star.

articles.title: Black Holes or Black Hole Stars? Astronomers Spar Over Webb Telescope’s ‘Little Red Dots.’
articles.description: The James Webb Space Telescope spots mysterious “little red dots” everywhere. A bold new theory suggests they’re suns dozens of times larger than our entire solar system. The post Black Holes or Black Hole Stars? Astronomers Spar Over Webb Telescope’s ‘Little…
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has discovered mysterious 'little red dots' throughout the cosmos, with astronomers debating whether they represent black holes or a new class of black hole stars. This discovery challenges existing understanding of early universe structure and stellar evolution.

articles.title: A Cosmic Catastrophe May Have Turned Neptune’s Ancient Moons Inside Out
articles.description: This image of the Neptune system, captured by the Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) on NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope in 2022, reveals stunning views of the planet’s rings—which have not been seen with this clarity in more than three decades—along with the pla…
articles.summary: New research suggests a cosmic catastrophe may have fundamentally altered Neptune's ancient moons, potentially flipping them inside out through dramatic gravitational interactions. This discovery, enabled by James Webb Space Telescope observations, reshapes our understanding of moon formation in the outer solar system.

articles.title: Te misje na Księżyc przejdą do historii. Nie tylko powrót ludzi
articles.description: Księżyc nie został zapomniany i obecnie trwa wyścig o Srebrny Glob. W ciągu najbliższych kilku lat czekają nas niezwykłe misje, których celem będzie naturalny satelita Ziemi. Wśród nich są Artemis IV agencji NASA czy chińska Chang'e 7, a na tym nie koniec. Na…
articles.summary: Multiple historic lunar missions are on the horizon as nations and organizations race to return humans to the Moon and establish sustained presence on the lunar surface. These upcoming missions represent a new era of lunar exploration with transformative scientific and technological significance.

articles.title: SpaceX to fly more NASA crews to space station under expanded $5.92 billion deal
articles.description: The deal brings SpaceX's ⁠total number of NASA astronaut flights under the contract to 17 and raises the contract's total value to $5.92 billion
articles.summary: SpaceX has secured an expanded $5.92 billion contract with NASA to conduct 17 crewed missions to the International Space Station. This landmark agreement underscores SpaceX's pivotal role in sustaining human spaceflight and advancing orbital operations.

articles.title: Perseverance’s View of ‘Turquoise Bay’
articles.description: Description NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover used its Mastcam-Z camera to capture this 360-degree panorama of “Turquoise Bay,” a geologic area of interest in the “Margin Unit.” The 818 images used to create the natural-color panorama were captured between Oct. 5 and Oct. 16, 2023, the 933rd to 944th Martian days, or sols, of the mission. […]
articles.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover captures a stunning 360-degree panorama of 'Turquoise Bay' on Mars using its Mastcam-Z camera.

articles.title: Juice to fly past Earth for third gravity assist
articles.description: The European Space Agency’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) will return to Earth on 28 September, with flight controllers guiding the spacecraft close to our home planet to alter its speed and direction en route to Jupiter.
articles.summary: ESA's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) successfully completes its third Earth gravity assist on September 28, advancing toward its Jupiter mission.

articles.title: A galaxy spinning out of sync
articles.description:
Image:
			
Though the spiral galaxy in this new image by the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope seems serene, it hides a chaotic secret. This galaxy is NGC 4698, and it lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. It’s one of over one thousand galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, the nearest large cluster of galaxies bound together by gravity.
As a spiral galaxy similar to our own Milky Way galaxy, NGC 4698 has spiral arms that curl around within a thin disc of stars, gas and dust. Its centre is dominated by a galactic bulge.
The diffuse off-white glow of the galaxy’s bulge comes from stars smaller, older, and cooler than the massive blue stars that dot the galaxy’s outer disc. These tightly packed stars orbit a supermassive black hole containing millions of times the Sun’s mass. Scientists have found signs that this black hole is actively growing, drawing gas inward with its gravitational pull.
With a flat, starry disc and diffusely glowing centre, NGC 4698 looks a lot like a typical spiral galaxy — but this galaxy is far from normal. NGC 4698 is one of only a few known spiral galaxies with a bulge that extends out from the disc at a right angle. The elongation is faintly visible in this Hubble image, which shows the ghostly glow of the starry bulge peeking above and below the dusty disc. What’s more, the stars and gas nearest the galaxy’s centre rotate perpendicular to the rest of the disc.
What could cause a galaxy to be so out of sync? Astronomers have found that the culprit likely lies outside the galaxy. If NGC 4698 funneled in gas from an outside source, the newly collected gas could have formed a disc of gas and stars in the galaxy’s centre, at an angle relative to the rest of the disc. Some observations suggest that this galaxy once experienced a minor galactic merger, as evidenced by a short ‘tail’ of hydrogen streaming from one side of the galaxy.
The data used to create this image come from an observing programme (#18103; PI: Thilker) focusing on galaxies in the Virgo Cluster.
[Image Description: A spiral galaxy viewed at an angle, with a bright central bulge and winding spiral arms. The arms form a ring around the galaxy, without appearing to reach its centre. Prominent red-brown dust lanes weave through the arms, which are also dotted with bright blue and reddish regions of star formation. The galaxy is set against a dark background scattered with stars and faint distant galaxies.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope reveals a spiral galaxy with unusual dynamics, showcasing the complexity and beauty of cosmic structures.

articles.title: Purple swirls on the Red Planet
articles.description: This image shows a prominent ice cliff near Mars’s south pole. With striking swirls of purple, pink and red, it’s a far cry from the colour palette we usually associate with the Red Planet.
articles.summary: Striking imagery of Mars's south polar ice cliff displays stunning purple, pink, and red swirls, revealing the planet's geological diversity.

articles.title: Hubble's superbubble scene
articles.description:
Image:
			
This sprawling cosmic vista and subject of today’s ESA/Hubble Picture of the Month comes from the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). The LMC is the largest of the small galaxies that orbit our Milky Way galaxy. At just 160 000 light-years away, the LMC offers a close look at highly active stellar birthsites like the nebula shown here. This nebula is named LHA 120-N44, or N44 for short, and it’s located in the constellation Dorado.
The appearance of this photogenic nebula is dominated by two features: a vast central void and a shell of dense, dusty gas. The central void is a ‘superbubble’ spanning roughly 210 by 140 light-years. The glittering stars at the centre of the void are responsible for its creation; through their powerful stellar winds and explosive supernovae, these stars have expelled much of the gas from which they were born.
When the stars of N44’s central star cluster swept away this gas, the expelled gas formed a shell around the superbubble. New stars are forming in this compressed gas shell, making N44 an interesting target for researchers studying the process of star formation. In particular, astronomers have turned to this nebula as an ideal place to time this process from start to finish. Their goal is to understand how long it takes from the collapse of cold gas clouds into dense knots to the moment nuclear fusion ignites in the heart of a newborn star.
Researchers used Hubble to survey N44 and take a census of its stars, cataloguing nearly half a million stars within the cluster as well as interlopers drifting in front of it. Of the stars surveyed, nearly 30 000 are what astronomers call pre-main-sequence stars, which have yet to begin fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores. This treasure trove of baby stars was discoverable thanks to the high sensitivity and fine spatial resolution of Hubble’s instruments that can pick out faint objects in crowded clusters.
The gas shell surrounding the superbubble is energised by ultraviolet radiation from massive stars, causing it to glow and highlighting several distinct features. Each feature within the broader N44 star-forming complex was catalogued by astronomer Karl Henize in the 1950s. One feature is a smaller bubble, catalogued as N44F, that is located near the upper-right corner of this image. N44F is an interstellar bubble blown by the intense stellar winds of a single hot and massive star. As this previously released Hubble closeup shows, the star’s furious winds and radiation have sculpted the surrounding bubble and created pillars of dusty gas.
The data used to create this image come from an observing programme (#14689; PI: Gouliermis) that aimed to probe stars in the N44 complex that have not yet begun fusing hydrogen into heavier elements in their cores. These data help to determine how long the process of star formation takes, as well as what masses newborn stars typically have. Hubble's sensitive observations of the lowest-mass stars in this region open a new window onto star formation in regions that, like the LMC or the galaxies of the early Universe, are poor in elements heavier than helium.
[Image Description: A dense field of stars fills the image, surrounded by wispy clouds of gas and dust. Pale blue and grey nebulosity forms an intricate web across the scene, with darker clouds of dust concentrated towards the lower right. Numerous bright stars appear in shades of blue, white and orange.]
articles.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope captures a magnificent cosmic vista of a superbubble in the Large Magellanic Cloud, revealing stellar dynamics and cosmic phenomena.

articles.title: Scientists Release Details About Moon's New Massive Crater
articles.description: It's easy to think of the Moon as the static constant companion in the night sky. Its face hasn’t visibly changed in millennia, and always faces us with the same side. But looks can be deceiving, as our closest companion is constantly bombarded by asteroids and comets that make small craters across the lunar landscape. While they might not be large enough for us to see with our naked eye, professional Moon watchers can pick up on them. And a recent paper published in Science Advances, describes the largest ever found in modern times.
articles.summary: Scientists have released detailed analysis of a newly discovered massive crater on the Moon, advancing our understanding of lunar geology and impact history.

articles.title: Astronomers Uncover "Hypersoft" X-ray Sources
articles.description: X-rays showcase some of the most unique astronomical objects in the universe. Neutron stars and black holes siphoning gas from companion stars stick out like sore thumbs at this level of radiation. However, according to a new paper by Mustafa Muhibullah and Jimmy Irwin from the University of Alabama and Rosanne Di Stefano from the Center for Astrophysics at Harvard & the Smithsonian, there appears to be another group of ultra-bright X-ray emitters that we’ve completely missed until now. They call them Hypersoft X-ray Sources (HSSs) and, according to a press release accompanying the paper, might answer two long-standing astronomical questions.
articles.summary: Astronomers have identified a new class of 'hypersoft' X-ray sources, expanding our knowledge of extreme cosmic objects and high-energy phenomena in the universe.

articles.title: The Sun Is Physically Capable of Producing a "Superflare" According To A New Study
articles.description: We have long known that the Sun is active. It “flares” quite often, sending huge amounts of energy off in a certain direction - sometimes directly at Earth. But we also know that, compared to other Sun-like stars, it seems relatively quiet, and not capable of producing the “superflares” we sometimes see in its stellar equivalents. That sounds like great news for humanity, and some scientists have even argued that lack of superflares was a critical impetus for the development of complex life on Earth. But a new paper from Natalie Krivova of the Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research and her co-authors in the journal Philosophical Transactions A calls the assumption that our Sun is incapable of such dramatic outbursts into question. That also means that, eventually, our highly technological society could bear the brunt of one of them.
articles.summary: New research confirms that the Sun is physically capable of producing superflares, enhancing our understanding of stellar activity and space weather phenomena.

articles.title: BepiColombo Makes Up-Close Measurement of Mercury's Solar Bombardment
articles.description: BepiColombo's measurements of particle bombardment at Mercury will help assess the impact of space storms on Mercury's surface and on Earth's atmosphere.
articles.summary: BepiColombo has made detailed measurements of particle bombardment at Mercury, providing valuable insights into space weather impacts on the solar system's innermost planet.

articles.title: Jupiter uses a surprisingly complex system to fend off particles from the sun
articles.description: A University of Iowa-led research team has reported in a new study the most detailed observations to date of the bow shock at Jupiter, our solar system's gas giant. The findings from NASA's Juno mission reveal key differences between Jupiter's bow shock and Earth's. They also may lead to a better understanding of the physics of how shocks function in even more powerful energy releases, such as those from dying stars. The research is published in Nature Communications.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: New research reveals that Jupiter employs a remarkably sophisticated system to protect itself from solar particles, demonstrating the complex magnetospheric dynamics of gas giants.

articles.title: A 'rebellious' exoplanet orbits in the opposite direction of its star
articles.description: A star and its planets form when a cloud of gas and dust collapses in on itself somewhere in space. The cloud then forms a disk around the nascent star, within which the planets will form. This protostar and its disk then rotate in the same direction.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered a remarkable 'rebellious' exoplanet that orbits in the opposite direction of its host star, challenging conventional planet formation theories.

articles.title: A giant crater may reveal the origin of Mars’ doomed moon
articles.description: A massive crater on Mars’ moon Phobos may hide a dense region of compressed material that could reveal whether the moon is a captured asteroid or debris from an ancient impact on Mars. Japan’s upcoming MMX sample return mission could provide the measurements and physical evidence needed to solve the mystery.
articles.summary: A massive crater on Mars' moon Phobos may contain clues about the moon's origin and composition through a dense region of compressed material.
